summary: G.I.G.A.S (Global Interactive Geographical Analytics System) is a free, open-source web app that shows how the Earth’s surface changes using radar data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite. It answers the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge by turning hard-to-read radar images and data into something anyone can explore and analyze. On a 3D globe, users can find floods, forest loss, wildfire scars, farmland changes and drying land, read a plain-language explanation of each one, and compare satellite photos from before and now. The system consists of two modes: Simple mode, written so a 10-year-old can follow it, and Technical mode, made for scientists and more experienced people. Both show data in English, Spanish and German, depending on what settings the user chose. The program holds value and matters because the radar sees past clouds, smoke and darkness, assessing threats and disasters when almost nobody sees them, and keeps record so it can reveal slow-moving patterns and problems early. NISAR, for example, measured parts of Mexico City sinking more than 2 cm a month. G.I.G.A.S puts that power in everyone’s hands.
details: G.I.G.A.S is a web app that shows how the Earth’s surface is changing, using radar from the NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite. Radar sends its own signal and listens for the echo, so it works at night and through clouds and smoke. Our system downloads only the needed pieces of NISAR data, finds places where the ground changed, and sorts each change into a simple category: floods, forest loss, wildfire scars, farming, growing cities, sinking ground or drying land. Each change comes with a confidence level and a plain explanation. Users spin a 3D globe, search any country or place, and open an area to see its radar pictures over time, a chart, and where every image comes from. They can also swipe between satellite photos from before and now, mark what changed between them, and download a PDF report. A “Happening now” panel adds live earthquakes, storms, fires and floods from official sources, always labeled as not radar. Simple mode explains everything in everyday words, and Technical mode shows every measurement; both work in English, Spanish and German. The benefit is that anyone, from students to farmers to local authorities, can understand what is happening to the land without being an expert. We hope this shows how useful NISAR data can be for everyday decisions, such as spotting flood damage, forest loss or sinking ground early. We built it with Python, FastAPI, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre and PDF tools, running on a Microsoft Azure server and Cloudflare. We combined NISAR with images from the VIIRS, Sentinel-2, Landsat and MODIS satellites, plus live public alert services. We wrote the code with Claude Code, and Meshy helped make the 3D satellite model. It is creative because it turns difficult radar into a friendly, explorable experience, with an animated welcome, a real 3D satellite model, and explanations with drawings. We considered accuracy (we never mix data of different quality levels, and we drop low-confidence detections), clear rules we can explain instead of a “black box”, honesty (nothing invented is shown as real), accessibility (colorblind-safe colors, keyboard use, reduced motion), and open-source credits and licenses.
